title: Treasure Map
solution_outline: P1: Equality of the two interpolations forces every grid depth to be a row factor plus a column factor. P2: Instead of constructing and traversing the known-depth graph, process equations online with weighted union-find. P3: Use a sparse difference-constraint graph with a hub to encode nonnegative row and column factors.

nodes.name: Equal interpolation means equal diagonal sums
nodes.statement: For a unit square with clockwise corners A,B,C,D, the two triangulated interpolations agree everywhere exactly when d(A)+d(C)=d(B)+d(D).
nodes.accept: At the center, the two interpolations are the averages of opposite corners, proving necessity. Equal diagonal sums make the four lifted corners coplanar, so both triangulations interpolate the same affine function, proving sufficiency.

nodes.name: Depths separate into row and column factors
nodes.statement: The unit-square equalities hold throughout the grid exactly when d(x,y)=r_x+c_y for some row factors r_x and column factors c_y. Every known depth therefore imposes r_x+c_y=d.
nodes.accept: The mixed discrete difference vanishes, so differences between neighboring rows are independent of the column. Equivalently, d(x,y)=d(x,1)+d(1,y)-d(1,1). Conversely, any row-plus-column representation satisfies all square equalities.

nodes.name: Nonnegative depths admit nonnegative factors
nodes.statement: A row-plus-column grid has nonnegative depth everywhere exactly when it has a representation d(x,y)=r_x+c_y with every r_x and c_y nonnegative.
nodes.accept: Nonnegative factors suffice. Conversely, shift the factors by subtracting min_x r_x from every row and adding it to every column. Rows become nonnegative, and each shifted column equals the minimum depth in that column. Linear interpolation also stays nonnegative.

nodes.name: Known-depth components have one shift
nodes.statement: In a connected component of the bipartite graph whose edges impose known-depth sums, any two satisfying assignments differ by adding one common shift to all row factors and subtracting it from all column factors. Thus any base solution (a,b) describes every solution as (a+s,b-s).
nodes.accept: Anchor one vertex at zero and propagate value(v)=d-value(u). Check every edge: a mismatch proves inconsistency; otherwise propagation supplies a base solution. Differences between satisfying assignments alternate sign across edges, leaving exactly one free shift per component, including isolated vertices. Iterative propagation takes O(n+m+k) time and space.

nodes.name: Component minima characterize feasibility
nodes.statement: For a consistent component, let A=min a_x over its rows and B=min b_y over its columns, with empty minima +∞. Nonnegative factors exist exactly when [-A,B] is nonempty. The map is feasible exactly when every component is consistent and has a nonempty interval.
nodes.accept: Rows require s>=-A and columns require s<=B. With both vertex types present this is A+B>=0; a one-sided component is always feasible. Components choose shifts independently, producing a globally nonnegative row-plus-column grid.

nodes.name: Component factor minima are attainable
nodes.statement: For a feasible component with base solution (a,b), let A=min_rows a_x and B=min_columns b_y. Among its nonnegative factor assignments, each row factor has minimum a_x-A and each column factor minimum b_y-B. These minima are attainable individually and independently across components.
nodes.accept: A row factor attains its minimum at s=-A, and a column factor at s=B. Both endpoints are permitted by component feasibility. Distinct components choose shifts independently; within one component, simultaneous attainment of both types of minima is not asserted. An isolated vertex has minimum factor zero.

nodes.name: Compute treasure depth from component labels
nodes.statement: Propagate the known-depth graph and output impossible for inconsistent equations or an empty component shift interval. Otherwise, output a_tx+b_ty if the treasure row and column share a component; if not, output (a_tx-A)+(b_ty-B), using each endpoint's own component minimum.
nodes.accept: Compute component labels, propagated values, and the two minima in O(n+m+k) time and space. Within one component the common shift cancels from the treasure sum; across components the endpoint minima are independently attainable. This also handles absent rows, absent columns, and an already-known treasure depth.

nodes.name: Depth insertion merges feasible shift intervals
nodes.statement: When a known-depth equation joins two consistent components, it fixes their relative shift. Their nonnegative solutions survive exactly when the translated shift intervals intersect. An equation inside one component is compatible exactly when it equals that component's fixed endpoint sum.
nodes.accept: Use signed potentials q(row)=r and q(column)=-c. If q(u)=t_A+delta_u and q(v)=t_B+delta_v, inserting q(u)-q(v)=d forces t_A-t_B=d-delta_u+delta_v. Translate one root's interval into the other's coordinate system and intersect. With equal roots, check delta_u-delta_v=d.

nodes.name: Maintain treasure feasibility with weighted union
nodes.statement: Insert known depths with weighted union-find, maintaining each root's admissible shift interval and rejecting inconsistent equations or empty intersections. If all insertions succeed, query the treasure endpoints: output their fixed sum when connected, or the sum of their independently minimum nonnegative factors otherwise.
nodes.accept: Initially signed row potentials have interval [0,infinity) and signed column potentials have interval (-infinity,0]. Maintain potential differences to parents, root intervals, and union by size with path compression. The connected answer is delta_row-delta_column; otherwise it is (delta_row+L_row)-(delta_column+U_column). Time is O((n+m+k) alpha(n+m)), space O(n+m).

nodes.name: Sparse hub graph encodes valid maps
nodes.statement: Let q(row)=r, q(column)=-c, and q(h)=0. An edge u→v with weight w imposes q(v)≤q(u)+w. Add column→row weight d and row→column weight -d for each known depth, plus row→h and h→column weight zero. These constraints represent precisely valid maps.
nodes.accept: The two edges for a known point enforce its equality. Hub edges enforce r>=0 and c>=0. By the nonnegative-factor characterization these impose precisely map feasibility, without materializing all n*m nonnegativity constraints. A common potential translation can always set the hub to zero.

nodes.name: Treasure minimum is a shortest-path bound
nodes.statement: If this constraint graph is feasible, the smallest treasure depth equals minus the shortest-path distance from treasure row to treasure column. The distance is finite, and its bound is attainable by assigning reachable potentials their source distances and extending to isolated unreachable rows.
nodes.accept: Every source-to-target path bounds q(target)-q(source) above by its length. There is always a path through the hub. Feasibility excludes negative cycles. Shortest distances satisfy every edge constraint on reachable vertices and attain the bound. Only isolated rows can be unreachable; give them sufficiently large potentials, then translate the hub to zero.

nodes.name: Feasible factors yield nonnegative path lengths
nodes.statement: Given feasible nonnegative factors r,c, reweighting the constraint graph by q=(r,-c,0) gives zero-weight known-depth edges, row-to-hub weights r_x, and hub-to-column weights c_y. All reduced weights are nonnegative, and reweighting preserves shortest paths between fixed endpoints.
nodes.accept: Use reduced edge weight w'(u,v)=w(u,v)+q(u)-q(v). Known-depth equalities make both corresponding reduced edges zero; the hub edges become the corresponding nonnegative factors. Potential differences telescope along each path, so all paths with the same endpoints gain the same constant and retain their relative lengths.

nodes.name: Optimize treasure depth using Dijkstra
nodes.statement: Propagate known-depth components, outputting impossible for contradictory equations or empty shift intervals. Otherwise choose admissible shifts, construct the nonnegative reweighted constraint graph, run Dijkstra from the treasure row, and output r_tx+c_ty minus the distance to the treasure column.
nodes.accept: Choose admissible component shifts, for example s=-A when rows exist. Dijkstra on zero-weight known-depth edges and factor-weighted hub edges computes D in O((n+m+k) log(n+m)) time and linear space. Telescoping gives D=dist_original+r_tx+c_ty. Since the optimum is -dist_original, output r_tx+c_ty-D.

end.statement: A solver holding every node of one END route can write a correct, fast enough program by routine coding; each route is an approach whose program the judge accepted.

hazards.statement: Intermediate factors and component bounds can exceed 32-bit range. Arithmetic must provide sufficient range and precision for reliable feasibility decisions and the exact integer output; unbounded endpoints must be handled safely.
hazards.check: Verify accumulated offsets, bounds, comparisons, and final rounding remain reliable over all inputs, including inconsistent ones. Signed 64-bit integers suffice; other representations qualify with justified error bounds. Ensure infinity representations cannot overflow or be mistaken for finite endpoints.

hazards.statement: The n by m grid can contain 9×10^10 points, and known-depth components can contain paths of linear length. Storage, work, and traversal depth must remain safe at these worst cases.
hazards.check: Reject worst-case dense-grid enumeration or storage. Sparse graphs may include auxiliary vertices and edges, as in the hub construction; weighted union-find also qualifies. Check that long components cannot exhaust the call stack or otherwise exceed the resource limits.

hazards.statement: A known treasure depth does not guarantee that the rest of the map is extendable.
hazards.check: Check consistency and nonnegative extendability in every component before reporting a numerical answer; output exactly impossible when any component fails.

hazards.statement: Rows and columns without known depths still participate in the map and may contain the treasure.
hazards.check: Represent isolated vertices explicitly or give absent coordinates equivalent zero-minimum unconstrained behavior. Do not require every component to contain both vertex types.

paths.approach: Equality of the two interpolations forces every grid depth to be a row factor plus a column factor. Nonnegativity of the entire grid is equivalent to choosing all factors nonnegative, so each connected component of the known-depth bipartite graph has an independent interval of allowed shifts. Propagating factors detects inconsistent equations; component minima then give feasibility and the minimum treasure depth in linear time.

Instead of constructing and traversing the known-depth graph, process equations online with weighted union-find. Each component carries its affine potentials and an admissible root-potential interval; a new equation either checks an existing difference or merges two components by translating and intersecting their intervals. This maintains exact feasibility in near-linear time and O(n+m) space, after which the treasure minimum follows from the endpoint components.

Use a sparse difference-constraint graph with a hub to encode nonnegative row and column factors. The minimum treasure depth is the negative shortest-path distance from its row to its column; a valid map obtained by component propagation reweights all graph edges to nonnegative lengths. Dijkstra then computes this extremal bound in O((n+m+k) log(n+m)) time, providing a shortest-path/duality approach rather than applying the componentwise minimum formula.

exploration.reason: Three distinct accepted paths cover direct component optimization, online weighted-union interval maintenance, and sparse difference-constraint shortest-path optimization. I do not have another genuinely different approach with a justified running time for the limits; the remaining ideas either reuse these same characterizations or are too expensive.
considered: Dense grid completion or Gaussian elimination: the grid can have 9e10 entries, and generic elimination on up to 600000 factors is unsuitable; sparse elimination reduces to the component-potential approach.

Bellman-Ford or SPFA on the sparse difference-constraint graph: Bellman-Ford is too slow in the worst case, and SPFA has no sufficient worst-case guarantee. Feasible-potential reweighting and Dijkstra are already represented by the accepted shortest-path path.
Binary search on the treasure depth: an efficient decision test reduces to the same component shift intervals and endpoint minima, adding repeated work rather than a genuinely new characterization.
Different graph traversals, spanning forests, or signed-potential conventions: these establish the existing propagation and component-minimum claims, so they do not constitute additional paths.

builder_notes: H1 now permits any numerical representation with sufficient range and justified precision, rather than requiring exact intermediate arithmetic. N12 now states only nonnegative reweighting and preservation of shortest paths; objective recovery is explained in N13. N6 is retained because removing or merging it would alter the fixed nodes and routes.
advisories: N6 (comes with its prerequisite; merge it): The minima and their attainability follow immediately by evaluating a_x+s and b_y-s at the endpoints of the interval established in N5; independence across components is also already established there. Fold this observation into N5's accept, rather than making it a separate stopping point.

order: Merge N6 into N5's accept and redirect dependencies on N6 to N5. The endpoint-minimization observation can also be referenced in N7 and N9; keeping existing node IDs and routes is not a substantive reason to retain this redundant step.
